newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - NI Electric profits hit by provisions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - NI Electric profits hit by provisions.

text.p: Regional utility Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) said on Friday that it had made "adequate" provisions to cover the costs of a tough pricing review as it turned in year pretax profits of 59.8 million pounds ($97.1 million).
"We have tried to reflect the severity of the review...our provisions are adequate," finance director Nigel Wilson told Reuters.
NIE said exceptional charges of 50.6 million pounds brought pretax profits for the year ending March 31 to 59.8 million from 107.4 million a year ago.
It paid out a total dividend of 20.9 pence per share, up from 19.0 pence previously.

NIE last month accepted a recommendation from the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) that prices should be cut by 25 percent this year, compared to a decrease of 31 percent proposed by its regulator Ofreg.
"We are taking immediate steps to meet the challenges set out in the new price controls," the company said in a statement with results.
NIE turned to the MMC last year in a high-profile row with Ofreg at the severity of the regulator's price proposals and the utility had expected the findings to be accepted by itself and Ofreg.
But when the MMC conclusions were announced on April 25, Ofreg took the unusual step of saying there were parts of the report's findings which it was "not...currently minded" to accept.

Wilson said NIE had written to Ofreg asking for clarification of its stance but was still awaiting a reply and said it was "disappointing" that there had been no meeting between the two since the MMC findings were published.

Wilson said the "cloud of financial uncertainty" from Ofreg's position as well as a possible "windfall" tax on utilities planned by the new Labour government meant NIE was unwilling to give any details on dividend growth or possible share buybacks.
"We shouldn't say more on dividends or share buybacks or capital restructuring...we would have liked to have," he said.

NIE said in its results statement that it was confident of delivering "real dividend growth" and said it would seek to renew its mandate to buy back up to 14.9 percent of shares at the annual meeting on July 4.
Wilson said NIE had not made provisions against a possible windfall tax from Labour because "there's too much uncertainty."

The Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory a week ago, has made a one-off windfall tax on utilities to be used to help young and long-term unemployed into work a key part of its programme.

But the government has given little indication of the size or scope of the tax, other than that it should cover the three billion pound scheme for the unemployed and will be aimed at the "excess" profits of privatised utilities.
Wilson said NIE's provisions included covering costs of the MMC review, relocation of staff, office closures and handling voluntary severance pay.
He declined to comment on potential job losses, saying talks with unions had just begun but stressing it was a voluntary process.

NIE said it was "determined" to meet the challenge of the MMC review, adding that although it was "a harsher result than the company's submission, it does provide NIE with real opportunities to build on our successes...in a manner not open to us under the Ofreg proposals."
